solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Drug cops out to keep it back

indicators.note: keeping something means holding it inside, so one piece sits within the other
going back means the combined letters are read from the end to the start

blocks.note: to cop out of something is to dodge or evade it
taken as written

explanation.surface: Police officers shirk their duty and hide some narcotic they seized.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cops' looks like police, but 'cops out' is the phrasal verb meaning to dodge a duty.
explanation.definitionFit: A sedative is a calming medicine, one particular kind of drug.

clue.text: Knocks up a wedge full of cold chicken

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means the word is read from bottom to top
being full of something means holding it inside

blocks.note: taps are light knocks
a chock is a wedge put against a wheel, as in 'chocks away'
C is the abbreviation for cold, as on taps

explanation.surface: Someone quickly makes a wedge-shaped sandwich packed with cold chicken.
explanation.walkthrough: A chock is the block wedged against an aircraft's wheels, hence 'chocks away'. 'full of' does double duty, with its 'of' also leading into the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A spatchcock is a chicken split open and flattened for grilling.

clue.text: Extremely dire rubbish about close relatives?

indicators.note: extremely points to the extremes of a word, its first and last letters
about means surrounding, so one word wraps round another

blocks.note: the outside letters of dire
pants is British slang for rubbish or nonsense
the close of something is its end

explanation.surface: Terrible nonsense spoken about one's next of kin.
explanation.walkthrough: Pants is British slang for rubbish. The question mark flags that dependants need not be relatives.
explanation.definitionFit: Dependants are people supported by someone, usually family members, so relatives by example.

clue.text: Farm tool creating lines in a row

indicators.note: in places one piece inside another

blocks.note: a tier is one row of a series stacked one above another
L is the abbreviation for line, doubled for the plural

explanation.surface: A piece of farm machinery that makes furrows in rows.
explanation.walkthrough: The two Ls go into the middle of TIER.
explanation.definitionFit: A tiller is a machine that breaks up and cultivates soil, used on farms and gardens.

clue.text: It appears to go on the face

definitions.text: It appears to go on the face

blocks.note: setter's reading: it seems to disappear, a thing that seems to depart
surface reading: a cosmetic applied to the skin of the face

explanation.walkthrough: Read 'appears to go' as 'seems to disappear': the product sinks into the skin so you can no longer see it.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a light cosmetic moisturiser that is absorbed into the skin leaving no visible trace.

clue.text: Leave work, given push

blocks.note: op. is short for opus, a musical work
to tout goods is to push or promote them hard

explanation.surface: Someone quits their job after being sacked or shoved out.
explanation.definitionFit: To opt out is to choose to withdraw from a scheme, i.e. to leave it.

clue.text: Drink up and linger for a piece of cake

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means the word for drink is read bottom to top

blocks.note: to sup is to drink
to hover is to linger or hang about

explanation.surface: Finish your drink and stay around to have a slice of cake.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a piece of cake' looks literal but is the idiom for something easy.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are informal idioms for a task or opponent that is very easy to beat.

clue.text: Order parts for old instrument

indicators.note: parting to make room for something means opening up so it can sit inside

blocks.note: the OBE is the Order of the British Empire
O is the abbreviation for old

explanation.surface: Someone orders spare parts for an antique musical instrument.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Order' looks like a verb about buying; it is the honour, OBE, which splits to admit O.
explanation.definitionFit: The oboe is a double-reed woodwind instrument.

clue.text: Can baby finally wee?

indicators.note: finally points to the closing letter of the word next to it

blocks.note: a tin is a can
the last letter of baby

explanation.surface: Is a baby able to pee at last?
explanation.walkthrough: 'Can' and 'wee' read as verbs about a toddler, but one is a container and the other a Scottish word for small.
explanation.definitionFit: Wee is a Scottish and informal word for small, a synonym of very small.

clue.text: Very fresh apricot goes in cake

indicators.note: fresh suggests something new, so these letters are made into a new arrangement

blocks.note: V is the abbreviation for very
taken as written, as anagram material

explanation.surface: A very ripe apricot is added to the cake mixture.
explanation.walkthrough: 'goes in' reads as an instruction to insert, but those words are part of the letters to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: A Victoria sponge is a classic British layered sponge cake with jam and cream.

clue.text: Dad getting over friend's outrage

indicators.note: getting over suggests flipping across, so the word for dad is turned round

blocks.note: pa is a familiar word for father
a pal is a friend

explanation.surface: A father recovering from a friend's furious behaviour.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's after friend stands for 'is', linking wordplay to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To outrage someone is to shock and appal them; both are transitive verbs of moral offence.

clue.text: Pinpoints rocky island that's private

indicators.note: rocky means unsteady or shaken about, so the letters are disturbed into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written, as anagram material
your own room is a private one, belonging to you alone

explanation.surface: A map locates exactly a craggy island in private ownership.
explanation.definitionFit: To nail something down is to establish it exactly, which is what pinpointing means.

clue.text: Turning around for a chat

indicators.note: going around something means enclosing it, so one word wraps another

blocks.note: a conversion is a turning, e.g. turning into something else
as in selling something at or for a price

explanation.surface: Spinning round in order to have a natter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a chat' is the definition, not part of the wordplay; AT sits between the S and I of the longer word.
explanation.definitionFit: A conversation is an informal talk between people, which is what a chat is.

clue.text: It may be a zombie — I'll return fire

indicators.note: to return is to go back, so the word for I is written backwards

blocks.note: I is the self; read 'I'll return' as 'I will be turned back'
an electric fire is a heater

explanation.surface: A zombie threatening to come back and shoot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fire' reads as a gunshot threat, but it is a domestic heater.
explanation.definitionFit: Zombies in horror films devour human flesh, so a zombie is one example of a flesh-eater.

clue.text: Plastic or, it's hoped, cloth?

indicators.note: plastic means easily moulded into a new shape, so the letters are remoulded

blocks.note: taken as written, as anagram material

explanation.surface: A wondering whether something is made of plastic or, one hopes, real fabric.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The cloth' is a standard term for the clergy, from clerical dress; the question mark admits the stretch.
explanation.definitionFit: The cloth is a figurative name for clergy, the body of priests collectively.

clue.text: Flatter type of cable

blocks.note: first meaning: to wheedle or cajole someone with praise
second meaning: short for coaxial cable, as used for TV aerials

explanation.surface: Describing a cable that is less bulky than another.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flatter' reads as the comparative adjective of flat, but it is the verb meaning to sweet-talk.
explanation.definitionFit: To coax is to persuade by gentle flattery; coax is also the everyday abbreviation of coaxial cable.

clue.text: Biker out in France, she runs German pub

indicators.note: out can mean disordered or wrong, so these letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written, as anagram material
elle is French for she
R is the cricket scoring abbreviation for runs

explanation.surface: A motorcyclist away in France while a woman manages a beer hall.
explanation.definitionFit: A bierkeller is a German beer cellar or tavern, i.e. a pub in the German style.

clue.text: Female need to have large mature body

blocks.note: F is the abbreviation for female
to have use for something is to need it
L is the clothing-size abbreviation for large
to age is to mature

explanation.surface: A woman wishing for a big, grown-up figure.
explanation.walkthrough: 'body' looks human, but it is the main body of an aircraft.
explanation.definitionFit: The fuselage is the main body of an aeroplane, holding crew, passengers and cargo.

clue.text: Petty thief?

blocks.note: surface reading: a small-time criminal who steals minor items
setter's reading: 'petty' as in pet-like, a thief named after a household pet

explanation.walkthrough: Petty usually means trivial; here it is read as relating to pets, and a cat is the classic pet.
explanation.definitionFit: This kind of burglar climbs walls and roofs with feline agility to break in.

clue.text: Man possibly heard in corridor

indicators.note: heard tells us to go by how the word sounds when spoken, not by spelling

blocks.note: an aisle is a passage or corridor between seats

explanation.surface: A man perhaps overheard talking in a hallway.
explanation.walkthrough: Man is the Isle of Man in the Irish Sea, so 'possibly' marks it as an example.
explanation.definitionFit: The Isle of Man is one example of an island, so Man is a possible instance.

clue.text: Man is one left to support old lady

indicators.note: in a down clue, supporting means sitting underneath, so this letter comes after

blocks.note: your old lady is informally your mother, mamma
L is the abbreviation for left

explanation.surface: A man is the one who stayed behind to care for his elderly mother.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Man is one' reads as a statement about a single man; it means the human species is an example.
explanation.definitionFit: Humans are mammals, warm-blooded animals that feed their young on milk.

clue.text: Future leader's great deal over Irish cause

indicators.note: lying over something can mean covering it all round, so one word encloses another

blocks.note: a heap of something is a great deal of it
Ir. is a standard abbreviation of Irish
the parent of something is its origin or cause

explanation.surface: The next leader has a big agreement concerning an Irish campaign.
explanation.walkthrough: 'great deal' suggests a bargain, but it means a large amount. The 's stands for 'is', a link.
explanation.definitionFit: The heir apparent is the person certain to succeed to a throne or top job.

clue.text: Small vehicle that one might pick?

blocks.note: S is the abbreviation for small
a cab is a taxi, a vehicle

explanation.surface: Choosing a compact car you might select.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pick' suggests choosing a car, but here it means picking at a healing wound.
explanation.definitionFit: A scab is the crust over a healing wound, which people are tempted to pick at.

clue.text: Miss or Mrs, initially the other

indicators.note: initially points to the opening letter of each of the words before it

blocks.note: the opening letters of or and Mrs
a bit of the other and it are both British euphemisms for sex

explanation.surface: A form asking for your title: Miss or Mrs, or else the other one.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Miss' looks like a title, but it is the verb meaning to leave out.
explanation.definitionFit: To omit something is to leave it out or fail to include it, the same as missing it.

clue.text: Please return what?

blocks.note: first meaning: a polite invitation to visit again
second meaning: a colloquial request to repeat something not heard

explanation.surface: Asking someone to come back and then saying 'pardon?'.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase works both literally, as a farewell to a guest, and as slang for 'say that again'.
explanation.definitionFit: Hosts and shops say it to invite a return, and people say it as an idiom for 'pardon?'.

clue.text: Saw too much within a second

indicators.note: within places one piece inside the other

blocks.note: a mo is a moment, a second
OTT is short for over the top, excessive

explanation.surface: Someone noticed too much in an instant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Saw' looks like the past tense of see, but it is the noun meaning an old saying.
explanation.definitionFit: A saw is a proverb or maxim, and a motto is a short guiding saying.

clue.text: British pure dairy product

blocks.note: B is the abbreviation for British
utter nonsense is pure nonsense; both mean complete

explanation.surface: A label describing a wholesome milk-based food from Britain.
explanation.definitionFit: Butter is made by churning cream, so it is a product of the dairy.

clue.text: Worried about unopened stock in wine store

indicators.note: something unopened has lost its opening, so the word's first letter goes
about means surrounding, so one word goes round another

blocks.note: to have cared about something is to have worried over it
to stock an item is to sell it; without its opening letter

explanation.surface: Someone fretted over unsealed supplies kept in a wine cellar.
explanation.walkthrough: A shop that stocks a product sells it; drop the first letter of that verb.
explanation.definitionFit: Cellared wine has been laid down and kept in a cellar, so it is in the wine store.
